cover imageThe Problem
When you open Instagram, a ranking system answers one question, millions of times per second, across billions of (user, content) pairs:
Given everything this user has ever done, everything their network has done, and every piece of content that exists — what are the ~500 items most worth showing next, in what order?
The “friend liked/commented, so I saw it” phenomenon we are experiencing is not a separate feature bolted onto the algorithm it’s one of several candidate generation sources that feed into a much larger pipeline. To understand it properly we need four subsystems working together:

• The Social Graph — who follows/is-connected-to whom, and edge “weights” (affinity)

• The Interaction/Event Pipeline — how a like/comment becomes a durable, Queryable fact

• Candidate Generation (Retrieval) — narrowing billions of posts down to a few thousand relevant ones per user

• Ranking (Scoring) — ML models that order those thousand candidates by predicted value
Let’s build this system layer by layer.
High-Level Architecture -

lets walk through this architecture .
The Social Graph: Who’s Connected to Whom -
Data Model -
Instagram’s social graph isn’t a single “friends” relationship — it’s several overlapping directed graphs:
This is naturally a graph, but at Instagram’s scale (billions of nodes, hundreds of billions of edges) you don’t run this on a traditional graph database like Neo4j for online serving — you use a sharded, denormalized graph store (conceptually similar to Meta’s TAO — “The Associations and Objects” system) where:

• Objects = users, posts, comments (immutable-ish entities with an ID)

• Associations = typed, directed edges with timestamps (user_likes_post, user_follows_user)
TAO sits on top of MySQL shards with a massive caching layer in front (originally memcache-based), because graph traversal at read time (e.g., “give me all posts my 500 followees liked in the last 6 hours”) must resolve in single-digit milliseconds.
Why a Graph Abstraction Specifically -
The key operation your article is really asking about — “a post my friend liked shows up for me” — is a 2-hop graph query:
me — follows → friend — liked → post
This is called Friend-of-Friend (FoF) propagation, and it’s one of the oldest and most powerful tricks in social recommendation, predating deep learning entirely (Facebook’s original “EdgeRank” from ~2010 was built almost entirely on this idea).
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Notice Reel #1 got liked by two of your friends (F1 and F2). This "signal stacking" matters a lot in ranking, which we'll formalize in Section 6.
The Event Pipeline: From Tap to Durable Fact -
When you double-tap a reel, here’s what happens before any recommendation logic even runs
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Key design decisions here, each of which is a real trade-off:

• Asynchronous write path. The like is acknowledged to your device instantly (optimistic UI), while the actual fan-out and processing happens in the background. This is why sometimes a like “un-registers” after a refresh — the async write occasionally races or gets deduplicated.

• Append-only event log. Interactions are never mutated in place; they’re appended to an immutable log (this is the same pattern as Kafka’s log-structured storage, or event sourcing). This lets multiple downstream consumers (graph store, ML feature pipelines, analytics) all read the same stream independently.

• Lambda architecture (batch + streaming). Two parallel paths process the same data:

• Speed layer (streaming): Flink/Storm-style jobs compute rolling windows — “how many likes has this post gotten in the last 10 minutes” — needed for surfacing trending content within minutes.

• Batch layer: Nightly/hourly Spark jobs recompute more expensive aggregates (full embedding retraining, long-window statistics) that don’t need sub-second freshness.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Candidate Generation: From Billions to Thousands -
This is the stage most people conflate with “the algorithm,” but it’s really the retrieval step — its entire job is to cheaply produce a manageable candidate pool (typically 1,000–5,000 posts) that the expensive ranking model will later score. There are usually 4–6 parallel retrieval sources, each specializing in a different signal type. Your “friend liked it” scenario is exactly one of these.
Source A — Friend-Activity Retrieval (the one you’re asking about)
Query pattern (conceptually, an approximation of what TAO-like systems execute):
-- Pseudocode, not literal SQL against a graph store
SELECT post_id, COUNT(DISTINCT actor_id) as friend_engagement_count,
ARRAY_AGG(actor_id) as which_friends
FROM interactions
WHERE actor_id IN (SELECT followee_id FROM follows WHERE follower_id = :me)
AND action_type IN ('like', 'comment', 'share')
AND timestamp > NOW() - INTERVAL '72 hours'
GROUP BY post_id
ORDER BY friend_engagement_count DESC
LIMIT 500At scale, this can’t literally be a live join across the whole graph every time you open the app — that would be too slow. Two engineering patterns solve this:
Fan-out-on-write:- When friend A likes a post, the system immediately pushes a pointer to that post into a precomputed “candidate inbox” for every one of A’s followers. Fast reads, expensive/wasteful writes (huge fan-out for high-follower accounts).
Fan-out-on-read:- Nothing is precomputed; when you open the app, the system does the 2-hop traversal live, pulling from your followers recent activity. Cheap writes, but read latency is higher and depends on how many people you follow.
Instagram (like Twitter/Facebook before it) uses a hybrid fan-out-on-write for typical users, fan-out-on-read (or a capped/sampled fan-out) for celebrity/high-degree accounts, to avoid a single popular like causing millions of writes.

Source B — Embedding-Based (ANN) Retrieval
This is the deep-learning half. Every user and every piece of content gets mapped into the same dense vector space (typically 64–512 dimensions) such that “relevant” pairs are close together, via a two-tower neural network:
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Why two towers and not one big model here? Because the item embeddings can be precomputed once for every post and stored in an Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) index (HNSW, IVF-PQ, ScaNN, FAISS-style structures). At request time, you only need to compute your user embedding once, then do a fast ANN lookup — O(log N)-ish instead of comparing against every item.
The math: the model is trained with a contrastive / softmax loss over positive and negative (user, item) pairs:
Since summing over the entire catalog V (hundreds of millions of items) is intractable, training uses sampled softmax or in-batch negatives:
where v+ is the positive (engaged) item and vi− are KK K sampled negatives (often other items in the same training batch — “in-batch negative sampling,” which is cheap because you get negatives for free from other users’ positives in the same minibatch).
Source C — Collaborative Filtering Retrieval
Classic “users who liked what you liked, also liked this.” Modeled via matrix factorization and we can factorize them like this
learned by minimizing regularized squared error over observed entries only:
Press enter or click to view image in full size

This is conceptually the ancestor of the two-tower neural model above — modern systems replaced the shallow bilinear factorization with deep networks, but the underlying idea (project users and items into a shared latent space) is the same.
Source D — Trending / Popularity Retrieval -
A simple velocity-based signal: content whose engagement rate is accelerating right now, regardless of your specific graph. Often modeled with something like:
Press enter or click to view image in full size

This is what powers Explore/Reels-tab discovery of content from accounts you don’t even follow.
Merging Candidate Sources -
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Each candidate typically carries a provenance tag — why it was retrieved (friend-liked, embedding-similar, trending, etc.) — because that provenance becomes an important feature in the ranking model, not just a debugging artifact.
Ranking: The Expensive, Precise Stage -
Retrieval answers “what’s plausibly relevant.” Ranking answers “in what exact order, and is it actually worth showing.” This is typically multi-stage because running a huge deep model on 2,500 candidates per user, times hundreds of millions of users, many times a day, is computationally enormous.

The Core Prediction Task -
The ranker doesn’t just predict “will they like it” — it predicts multiple actions simultaneously via a multi-task neural network, because “value” is genuinely multi-dimensional:
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Each of these is typically a binary classification (or regression, for watch time) head sharing a common trunk of layers:
Press enter or click to view image in full size

The final score is a weighted combination, tuned to reflect product priorities (this weighting is itself a huge lever product/growth teams pull):
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Where “Friend Liked This” Enters the Ranking Math -
This is the crux of your article’s premise: the friend-signal isn’t just a retrieval trick — it re-appears as an explicit feature at ranking time, formalized in something close to the original EdgeRank-style formula (still conceptually alive inside modern systems, just now one input among thousands to a neural net rather than the whole algorithm):
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Where:

• Affinity(u, f) — a learned score of how much uu u actually interacts with friend ff f (DMs, profile visits, comment reciprocity) — not just the follow edge. This itself is often a small logistic regression or gradient-boosted tree over interaction-frequency features.

• Weight(action) — comments generally weighted higher than likes (higher intent), shares highest.

• Decay(t) — a time-decay function, typically exponential:
so a friend’s like from 2 hours ago counts more than one from 2 days ago.
Two friends liking the same post doesn’t just linearly add — it also acts as a strong feature interaction the neural ranker learns implicitly (e.g., “multiple independent friends engaging” correlates with genuinely higher quality/relevance, a weak form of crowd-sourced quality signal, similar in spirit to page-rank-style endorsement).
Loss Function for Each Head -
Each binary head (e.g., P(like)) is trained with standard binary cross-entropy:
Press enter or click to view image in full size

and the multi-task total loss is a weighted sum across heads:
with αk ​ tuned per task (often via techniques like uncertainty weighting so tasks with noisier labels don’t dominate training).
Re-Ranking: Diversity, Exploration, and Guardrails -
A pure top-K-by-score feed would be extremely repetitive (e.g., ten reels from the same friend in a row, or all from one content category). The final re-ranking stage applies:

• Diversity constraints — e.g., Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR)-style penalization:
Press enter or click to view image in full size

This discourages showing near-duplicate content back-to-back even if both scored well.

• Exploration / exploitation trade-off — the system deliberately injects some lower-confidence candidates to keep learning about your preferences and avoid filter bubbles feeding on themselves. This is a classic multi-armed bandit problem, often solved with Thompson Sampling:

• Each candidate’s score is modeled as a distribution (not a point estimate), e.g., Beta(α, β) for a click-through rate.

• You sample from each distribution and rank by the sampled value (not the mean), naturally balancing “confident good bets” with “under-explored, possibly great content.”
